title: Memory--Transport Competition in Physical Two-Bath Quantum Reset Dynamics
authors: Jishad Kumar, Achilleas Lazarides, Tapio Ala-Nissila
abstract: Coherence preservation and environmental renewal offer competing ways of controlling quantum memory and transport. We show that a seemingly natural protocol which exactly replaces the bath occupations while preserving arbitrary system--bath coherences need not correspond to a physical fermionic state. We instead construct a two-reservoir protocol with independent, number-conserving thermal attenuators, for which complete positivity and fermionic admissibility hold by construction. Physical attenuation necessarily modifies bath populations as well as cross correlations; the coherence control is not an independent hard-reset knob. Quadratic dynamics reduces the stroboscopic problem to an exact matrix fixed-point equation without a weak-coupling or Markov approximation. Analytically, coherence retention enhances the leading short-cycle transfer rate, including the complete-erasure limit; no general endpoint-vanishing theorem exists. An exact stationary continuity theorem forces the through-current to vanish whenever either reservoir is left entirely unrefreshed, although no analogous theorem suppresses it at complete erasure. For biased structured reservoirs, exact finite-chain calculations display distinct coherence-, current-, and signed energy-transfer operating points; a resolved high-retention boundary layer exposes strong finite-size sensitivity of the coherence peak. The model provides a microscopic, fermion-admissible benchmark for the interplay of reservoir coherence, particle transport, and energetic exchange.
summary: This paper analyzes quantum memory and transport in a fermionic system coupled to two baths undergoing periodic resets. It shows that coherence control is not an independent knob, and it derives a fundamental entropy balance equation governing the system's steady-state dynamics. This provides a rigorous theoretical framework for understanding energy and information exchange in open quantum systems.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental competition between preserving quantum coherence (memory) and facilitating particle transport in quantum systems subjected to periodic environmental resets.
main_result: The authors establish that physical reset protocols are constrained by requirements like complete positivity, and they derive an exact entropy balance identity linking entropy production to mutual information and quantum relative entropy.
method: The analysis employs exact, non-approximative methods using the one-particle density matrix (SPDM) evolution, solving discrete Lyapunov equations for the stationary state.
model_or_system: The model is a fermionic system coupled to two structured baths (Left and Right reservoirs) undergoing periodic unitary evolution followed by a number-conserving thermal attenuation/refresh cycle.
key_observables: Coherence norm, particle throughput (through-current), signed energy transfer, entropy production, mutual information, and quantum relative entropy.
important_parameters: Attenuation parameters ($\eta_a$), temperature/chemical potential ($ eta, \mu_a$), and the cycle period ($	au$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on constructing a physically admissible, number-conserving two-bath protocol, distinguishing it from formal hard-reset prescriptions.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the dynamics via the SPDM evolution, deriving the stationary state via fixed-point equations, and culminating in the rigorous derivation and application of an exact entropy balance identity.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, microscopic benchmark for open quantum systems, directly addressing the non-trivial interplay between coherence preservation and energy/particle flow in non-equilibrium steady states.

From left to right: retained system–bath coherence Cmem, particle-current magnitude |JN|, and signed energy-transfer rate JE into the outgoing thermal ancillas. The black marker in each panel denotes the maximum on the displayed 41 × 41 parameter grid. All stationary covariances satisfy 0 ≤C ≤I. The parameter range is restricted to 0 ≤ηa ≤0.995; the nonrefreshing endpoint ηa = 1 is not included.

Left: retained coherence, particle-current magnitude, and signed energy-transfer rate along ηL = ηR, each divided by its maximum along that cut to compare the locations of the extrema. Right: mode-resolved coherence weights |C0,ak|2 for the left and right reservoirs at the two-parameter current optimum (ηL, ηR) = (0.5224, 0.8955).

FIG. 3. Bath-size dependence of the stationary observables for the Gaussian partial-refresh protocol. The retention parameters are held fixed at the respective Na = 28 grid maxima listed in Eq. (34). From left to right: retained coherence Cmem, particle- current magnitude |JN|, and signed energy-transfer rate JE. The legend in the left panel applies to all three panels.

FIG. 4. High-retention behavior of the stationary coherence Cmem for several reservoir lengths NL = NR = Na, at fixed ηL = 0.42529. The coherence has a narrow maximum within 0.97 ≤ηR ≤1 that shifts toward full retention as Na increases. This maximum lies outside the range ηR ≤0.995 used for the operating landscape in Fig. 1.

FIG. 5. Fermionic admissibility domain of the algebraic hard- block prescription. Yellow indicates post-reset fixed points satisfying both Schur-complement inequalities (37) and (38); dark indicates their violation. The cross marks a repre- sentative algebraic transport operating point that fails the fermionic admissibility test. The figure is computed from the corresponding affine algebraic map using NL = NR = 28.
